summary: For ages 6-7 (Y1/Y2): add and subtract within 20 using strategies — making ten (8+6 = 8+2+4 = 14), decomposing to bridge ten (13−4 = 13−3−1 = 9), and deriving from known facts. The core insight is treating ten as a friendly landmark reached in both directions; this bridging reasoning later underpins column carrying and borrowing. The focus is the method, not just a correct answer, since counting all by ones can reach 14 without showing the intended understanding.
misconceptions: Counting on/back in ones across ten instead of using ten as a landmark (slow and error-prone at the boundary).
Splitting the wrong addend or splitting it wrongly when making ten (e.g. taking 4 not 2 from the 6 to fill an 8).
For subtraction, decomposing incorrectly across ten (13−4 done as 13−4 in ones with a boundary error).
Not connecting making-ten to known bonds to 10, so the strategy feels arbitrary.
Applying making-ten rigidly even when a known fact or near-double would be quicker.

activities.title: Make ten by moving counters on a double ten-frame
steps: Set out 8 counters in the first ten-frame (two cells empty) and 6 in the second to add 8 + 6.
Move 2 counters from the 6 across to fill the first frame to 10, and notice the 6 has broken into 2 and 4.
Read the result as 10 + 4 = 14, and say aloud which part you moved and why.
Record the same move on an empty number line as a jump of +2 to reach 10, then +4 to reach 14.
Repeat with other bridging facts (e.g. 7+5, 9+6), each time completing the first ten first.
activities.insight: Making ten is a MOVE: reorganising an awkward fact around the friendly ten (8+6 becomes 10+4) shows WHY the strategy works, not just that it gives 14.

activities.title: Bridge down to ten for subtraction
steps: To work out 13 − 4, start at 13 and first subtract enough to land on 10: 13 − 3 = 10.
Then subtract the rest: the 4 was split into 3 and 1, so take the remaining 1, giving 10 − 1 = 9.
Show both jumps back on a number line — back to 10, then one more past it.
Check you have subtracted the whole amount (3 + 1 = 4), not just part of it.
Try more subtractions that cross ten (12−5, 15−7), each time stepping onto ten first.
activities.insight: Ten is a landmark in BOTH directions: decomposing the number being subtracted so you land on ten first keeps the calculation accurate across the boundary.

activities.title: Explain and compare strategies aloud
steps: Talk through how you worked out 8 + 6, step by step: which number did you split, and what did that make?
Answer probing questions: 'Why did you take 2 across to the 8 — what does that make?' and 'For 13 − 4, why break the 4 into 3 and 1?'
Offer a second method for 8 + 6 (e.g. treat it as a near-double: move 1 from the 8 to the 6 to make the double 7 + 7 = 14, or use 6 + 6 + 2, or a known fact) and say which felt quicker.
Use a known addition fact to derive a subtraction: if 8 + 4 = 12, explain how that gives 12 − 8 = 4.
Describe how a ten-frame shows what is happening in your method.
activities.insight: Because this is a reasoning strategy, explaining and comparing methods builds flexibility — children learn to choose making-ten, a near-double or a known fact according to the calculation, and to see addition and subtraction as related.

activities.title: Fill the bridging step
steps: Complete the make-ten decomposition: 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + ___ , then give the total.
Complete a subtraction decomposition: 13 − 4 = 13 − 3 − ___ , then give the answer.
Say which number got split and why that amount was chosen.
activities.insight: Recording the intermediate bridging step makes the strategy's structure explicit and checkable.

checkQuestion: Show me how you work out 8 + 6 — talk me through your steps. Now do 13 − 4 and tell me how.
checkAnswer: 8 + 6 = 14 via make-ten (8 + 2 = 10, then + 4 → 14); 13 − 4 = 9 via decomposing to ten (13 − 3 = 10, then − 1 → 9). Any valid bridging strategy is fine — the point is a strategy, not counting all.
